explicit_validation.explanation: Paper explicitly compares LLM-as-judge binary factual consistency predictions against human-annotated ground truth labels using quantitative metrics (balanced accuracy) on the same set of summary sentences and summaries

prompts.notes: Paper mentions using zero-shot prompts for binary factual consistency prediction (DIR method) and chain-of-thought prompts for explanations (EXP method). Full prompts are referenced as being in Appendix C.3.

guidelines.notes: Full annotation instructions and interfaces described in Appendix F, including definitions for factual consistency, relevance, completeness, and error taxonomy with examples

sample_size.notes: Validation uses all 3,966 summary sentences in the test set (30% split of benchmark), covering both main-topic (75%) and marginal-topic (25%) summaries

quantitative_scores.value: surpasses non-LLM metrics only for GPT-4
quantitative_scores.notes: GPT-4 achieves best performance; other LLMs perform poorly compared to non-LLM metrics

quantitative_scores.value: non-LLM metrics capture all error types better
quantitative_scores.notes: Non-LLM metrics outperform LLMs at detecting diverse error types, especially for nuanced meaning shift and contradiction errors
Non-LLM metrics produce frequent false alarms, while LLMs have higher false negative rates

validation_results.summary_finding: LLM-as-judge performs poorly on factual consistency evaluation in dialogue summarization domain; non-LLM specialized metrics outperform most LLMs except GPT-4, which shows moderate alignment with human judgments

criteria_mapping.notes: Both LLM and human evaluate binary factual consistency at sentence level; human evaluation covers additional dimensions not assessed by LLMs
